questions.questionText: What is supervised machine learning?

options.text: Training a model on unlabelled data to discover patterns
Training a model on labelled data where the correct answers are provided
Training a model through trial and error using rewards and penalties
Training a model by having humans supervise the process at each step

explanation.correct: Supervised learning uses labelled training data â€” each example has input features and a known correct output (label). The model learns to map inputs to outputs.
explanation.incorrect: Unlabelled data = unsupervised learning. Rewards/penalties = reinforcement learning. Human supervision of each step is not the definition.
explanation.examTip: Supervised = labelled data (you know the answers). Unsupervised = unlabelled data (discover patterns). Reinforcement = learn by rewards.

questions.questionText: Which machine learning technique trains a model by having it interact with an environment, receiving rewards for correct actions?

options.text: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Transfer learning

explanation.correct: Reinforcement learning trains an agent to make decisions by rewarding correct actions and penalising incorrect ones â€” used in game playing, robotics, and autonomous systems.
explanation.incorrect: Supervised = labelled data. Unsupervised = finding patterns. Transfer = using a pre-trained model on a new task.
explanation.examTip: Reinforcement learning examples: game-playing AI (chess, Go), robot navigation, recommendation systems optimisation.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a training dataset in machine learning?

options.text: To evaluate the final performance of a trained model on unseen data
To teach the model by exposing it to examples so it can learn patterns
To fine-tune hyperparameters during model development
To monitor model performance after deployment

explanation.correct: The training dataset is used to teach the model â€” it's exposed to many examples so it learns the patterns and relationships between inputs and outputs.
explanation.incorrect: Evaluating final performance = test dataset. Hyperparameter tuning = validation dataset. Post-deployment monitoring = separate process.
explanation.examTip: Data splits: Training (teach the model) â†’ Validation (tune hyperparameters) â†’ Test (evaluate final performance). Never use test data during training.

questions.questionText: What does 'overfitting' mean in machine learning?

options.text: The model performs poorly on both training and test data
The model learns the training data too well, including noise, and performs poorly on new data
The model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data
The training process takes too long due to excessive data

explanation.correct: Overfitting occurs when a model memorises the training data (including noise) rather than learning general patterns, resulting in high training accuracy but poor performance on new unseen data.
explanation.incorrect: Poor on both = underfitting. Too simple = underfitting. Training time is not overfitting.
explanation.examTip: Overfitting = high train accuracy, low test accuracy (too complex). Underfitting = low train and test accuracy (too simple). Goal = balance (generalisation).

questions.questionText: What is Azure Machine Learning used for?

options.text: Managing Azure virtual machines and cloud infrastructure
Building, training, deploying, and managing machine learning models at scale
Storing and querying large datasets in the cloud
Creating and managing Azure Active Directory users

explanation.correct: Azure Machine Learning is a cloud platform for the full ML lifecycle â€” data preparation, model training, hyperparameter tuning, deployment as web services, and monitoring.
explanation.incorrect: VM management = Azure Resource Manager. Data storage = Azure Storage/SQL. Identity = Entra ID.
explanation.examTip: Azure ML key features: designer (no-code), automated ML (AutoML), notebooks, pipelines, model registry, managed endpoints.

questions.questionText: What is Automated ML (AutoML) in Azure Machine Learning?

options.text: A feature that automatically deploys models to production without human review
A feature that automatically tries multiple algorithms and hyperparameters to find the best model for a dataset
An automated process for collecting and labelling training data
A tool that automatically writes Python code for machine learning

explanation.correct: AutoML automates the model selection and hyperparameter tuning process â€” it iterates through many algorithm/parameter combinations and returns the best performing model, reducing the need for deep ML expertise.
explanation.incorrect: AutoML finds the best model, it doesn't auto-deploy, label data, or write code.
explanation.examTip: AutoML is ideal for non-ML experts who want to quickly build models. It handles algorithm selection, feature engineering, and hyperparameter tuning automatically.

questions.questionText: Which model evaluation metric measures the percentage of correct predictions out of all predictions made?

options.text: Precision
Recall
Accuracy
AUC

explanation.correct: Accuracy = (correct predictions) / (total predictions). It measures overall correctness across all classes.
explanation.incorrect: Precision = correct positive predictions / all positive predictions. Recall = correct positives / all actual positives. AUC = area under ROC curve.
explanation.examTip: Accuracy is misleading with imbalanced data. If 95% of emails are not spam, a model that predicts 'not spam' always achieves 95% accuracy but is useless.

questions.scenarioText: A medical AI model is used to screen patients for a serious disease. The model has high accuracy but frequently misses positive cases (people who have the disease).
questions.questionText: Which metric should be prioritised to reduce missed positive cases?

options.text: Accuracy
Precision
Recall (Sensitivity)
Specificity

explanation.correct: Recall (sensitivity) measures how many actual positive cases the model correctly identifies. In disease screening, missing a positive case (false negative) is dangerous â€” high recall minimises missed diagnoses.
explanation.incorrect: Accuracy is misleading with imbalanced medical data. Precision measures false positives, not misses. Specificity measures true negatives.
explanation.examTip: Medical screening = maximise Recall (catch all sick people). Spam filter = maximise Precision (don't block legitimate emails). High-stakes = recall. False alarms acceptable = recall. Wrong positives costly = precision.

questions.questionText: What does the Azure Machine Learning Designer provide?

options.text: A command-line interface for training models in Azure
A visual drag-and-drop interface for building ML pipelines without writing code
A pre-built model library for common business scenarios
An automated tool for deploying models to edge devices

explanation.correct: Azure ML Designer is a visual canvas where you connect dataset and module components to build, train, and deploy ML pipelines â€” no code required, ideal for non-developers.
explanation.incorrect: CLI = Azure ML CLI. Pre-built models = Azure AI Services. Edge deployment = Azure IoT Edge/ONNX.
explanation.examTip: Azure ML Designer = visual/drag-drop (no code). Azure ML notebooks = code-based (Python). AutoML = automated algorithm selection.

questions.questionText: What is a feature in the context of machine learning?

options.text: The final output prediction made by the model
An individual measurable input variable used to train a model
A new capability added to an AI product
The accuracy score of a trained model

explanation.correct: A feature is an individual measurable input variable (attribute) used by the model for training and prediction. For a house price model, features might be: square footage, number of bedrooms, location.
explanation.incorrect: Output = label. Product capability = product feature (different context). Accuracy = evaluation metric.
explanation.examTip: Features = inputs (X). Labels = outputs (Y). Feature engineering = creating better features from raw data to improve model performance.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Azure Machine Learning concepts.

statements.text: An Azure ML workspace is the top-level resource that contains all ML assets including experiments, models, and datasets.
Azure ML compute clusters can only run on a single virtual machine.
A model endpoint in Azure ML allows applications to send data and receive predictions.
AutoML requires users to specify which algorithm to use before training begins.

explanation.correct: Workspace = top-level container for all ML resources. Endpoints = inference APIs. Compute clusters = multi-node scalable compute. AutoML = automatically selects algorithms, no user specification needed.
explanation.incorrect: Compute clusters can scale across many nodes. AutoML's whole purpose is to try many algorithms automatically.
explanation.examTip: Azure ML workspace contains: datasets, experiments, models, endpoints, compute, environments, pipelines.

questions.questionText: What does Azure Machine Learning's model registry do?

options.text: It automatically trains models on a schedule
It provides a centralised store to version, track, and manage trained ML models
It registers Azure subscription quotas for ML compute
It stores training datasets for reuse across experiments

explanation.correct: The model registry stores trained model files with version numbers, metadata, performance metrics, and lineage information â€” enabling teams to track, compare, and promote models through environments (dev â†’ staging â†’ production).
explanation.incorrect: Scheduled training = ML pipelines. Quotas = Azure subscription management. Datasets are stored in data assets, not the model registry.
explanation.examTip: Model registry = central store for model versions. Track: version, metrics, training run, dataset used. Promote winning models to deployment.

questions.questionText: What is a confusion matrix used for in machine learning?

options.text: To visualise the structure of a neural network
To evaluate a classification model by showing counts of correct and incorrect predictions for each class
To compare training and validation loss during model training
To display the importance of each feature in a model

explanation.correct: A confusion matrix shows the counts of True Positives, True Negatives, False Positives, and False Negatives for a classifier â€” revealing exactly which classes the model confuses with others.
explanation.incorrect: Network visualisation = different tools. Training/validation curves = loss plots. Feature importance = separate chart.
explanation.examTip: Confusion matrix: TP (correct positive), TN (correct negative), FP (false alarm), FN (missed positive). From it you calculate accuracy, precision, recall, F1.

questions.questionText: Place the steps of a typical machine learning workflow in the correct order.

orderItems.text: Define the problem and gather data
Prepare and clean the data (feature engineering)
Train the model on training data
Evaluate the model on test data
Deploy the model as a service

explanation.correct: ML lifecycle: Define problem â†’ Prepare data â†’ Train â†’ Evaluate â†’ Deploy â†’ Monitor. This mirrors CRISP-DM and Azure ML's process.
explanation.incorrect: Data must be prepared before training. Evaluation comes after training. Deployment follows evaluation. Monitoring is ongoing after deployment.
explanation.examTip: This ML lifecycle is a recurring exam topic. Azure ML supports all these steps in one platform.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of cross-validation in machine learning?

options.text: To validate that the model code has no syntax errors
To get a more reliable estimate of model performance by training and evaluating on multiple data splits
To check that training and test data come from the same distribution
To validate that all features are normalised before training

explanation.correct: Cross-validation (e.g., k-fold) splits data into k subsets, trains on k-1, tests on 1, rotates through all combinations, and averages results â€” giving a more reliable performance estimate than a single train/test split.
explanation.incorrect: Cross-validation is about model evaluation reliability, not code validation, distribution checks, or data preprocessing.
explanation.examTip: k-fold cross-validation: split into k folds, train k times (each time using a different fold as test), average results. Reduces evaluation variance.

questions.questionText: What is transfer learning?

options.text: Moving a trained model from one Azure region to another
Reusing a model trained on a large dataset as the starting point for training on a smaller related task
Transferring training data between different ML frameworks
Copying model weights between different team members

explanation.correct: Transfer learning takes a model pre-trained on a large general dataset (e.g., ImageNet for images, GPT for text) and fine-tunes it on a smaller domain-specific dataset â€” saving time and compute while achieving good results.
explanation.incorrect: Transfer learning is an AI technique, not a data migration, framework conversion, or file sharing process.
explanation.examTip: Transfer learning enables: training custom image classifiers with few examples (Custom Vision), fine-tuning LLMs on domain data. Pre-trained â†’ fine-tuned on your data.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of normalisation/scaling in machine learning data preparation?

options.text: To remove duplicate records from the training dataset
To bring features onto a similar scale so no single feature dominates model training
To convert categorical features into text labels
To split the dataset into training and test sets

explanation.correct: Normalisation (0-1 range) or standardisation (mean 0, std 1) ensures features with large scales (e.g., salary: 50,000) don't dominate over features with small scales (e.g., age: 35) during model training.
explanation.incorrect: Deduplication removes duplicates. One-hot encoding = categorical to numerical. Train/test split = data partitioning.
explanation.examTip: Feature scaling matters for: gradient descent-based models, k-NN, SVMs, neural networks. Tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost) don't require scaling.

questions.scenarioText: A data scientist trains a model that achieves 99% accuracy on training data but only 62% accuracy on the test set.
questions.questionText: What is MOST likely happening and what should be done?

options.text: The model is underfitting â€” more training data is needed
The model is overfitting â€” regularisation, more data, or a simpler model should be tried
The model is performing well â€” 62% test accuracy is acceptable
The test data is corrupted and should be replaced

explanation.correct: High train accuracy (99%) with low test accuracy (62%) is a classic overfitting signature â€” the model memorised the training data. Solutions: add regularisation (L1/L2, dropout), get more training data, simplify the model, or use early stopping.
explanation.incorrect: Underfitting = low accuracy on both train AND test. 62% test accuracy with 99% train is clearly overfitting. Test data corruption is unlikely to cause this specific pattern.
explanation.examTip: Overfitting fix: more data, regularisation, dropout (neural nets), pruning (trees), simpler model, data augmentation, cross-validation.

questions.questionText: What is data labelling in the context of supervised machine learning?

options.text: Adding column headers to a CSV dataset
Annotating training examples with the correct output (class, value, or bounding box) for the model to learn from
Assigning version numbers to trained models
Tagging Azure resources for cost management

explanation.correct: Data labelling (annotation) is the process of adding correct output labels to training data â€” e.g., marking images as 'cat' or 'dog', drawing bounding boxes around objects, or tagging text with sentiment.
explanation.incorrect: CSV headers = data schema. Model versioning = MLOps. Resource tags = Azure cost management.
explanation.examTip: Azure ML Data Labelling is a service for crowdsourcing and managing labelling projects. Quality and quantity of labels directly impacts model performance.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Azure Machine Learning model monitoring feature after deployment?

options.text: To retrain the model automatically when accuracy drops
To detect data drift and performance degradation in production, alerting when the model needs retraining
To monitor Azure infrastructure costs for the ML workload
To provide audit trails for regulatory compliance

explanation.correct: Model monitoring tracks data drift (input distribution change), concept drift (relationship between inputs and outputs changes), and performance metrics â€” alerting teams when the deployed model needs retraining.
explanation.incorrect: Auto-retraining is a separate pipeline. Cost monitoring = Azure Cost Management. Compliance auditing = separate tools.
explanation.examTip: Data drift: training data distribution â‰  production data distribution over time. Causes model degradation. Monitor â†’ detect drift â†’ retrain cycle.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between batch inferencing and real-time inferencing in Azure Machine Learning?

options.text: Batch runs faster than real-time
Batch processes large volumes of data asynchronously; real-time returns instant predictions for individual requests
Real-time only works with tabular data; batch works with images
They are the same but run in different Azure regions

explanation.correct: Batch inferencing processes large datasets in bulk (e.g., score all customers overnight). Real-time inferencing responds immediately to individual requests (e.g., fraud check at point of payment).
explanation.incorrect: Real-time is faster per request but batch has higher throughput. Both support various data types. They serve different use cases.
explanation.examTip: Batch = high volume, latency tolerable (reports, recommendations). Real-time = immediate response needed (fraud, recommendations at click-time, medical alerts).

questions.questionText: What is the primary benefit of using Azure Machine Learning pipelines?

options.text: They automatically select the best ML algorithm for a dataset
They orchestrate reusable, automated workflows for data preparation, training, evaluation, and deployment
They provide a visual interface for data scientists to explore datasets
They manage cost allocation for ML compute resources

explanation.correct: Azure ML pipelines automate the end-to-end ML workflow as a series of steps â€” data preprocessing, training, evaluation, registration â€” that can be scheduled, reused, and versioned for reproducibility.
explanation.incorrect: Algorithm selection = AutoML. Visual exploration = Azure ML Designer/notebooks. Cost management = Azure Cost Management.
explanation.examTip: ML pipelines = automation + reproducibility + reusability. Each step can be run independently. Re-run only changed steps for efficiency.

questions.questionText: What is MLOps and why is it important?

options.text: A machine learning technique for optimising model hyperparameters
The practice of applying DevOps principles to ML to automate and manage the ML lifecycle reliably and at scale
A cloud service for deploying ML models to edge devices
A method for labelling large datasets using crowdsourcing

explanation.correct: MLOps (ML + DevOps) applies CI/CD principles to machine learning â€” automating training pipelines, model versioning, testing, deployment, and monitoring to make ML production-ready and maintainable.
explanation.incorrect: Hyperparameter tuning = AutoML/grid search. Edge deployment = Azure IoT Edge/ONNX. Data labelling = annotation tools.
explanation.examTip: MLOps lifecycle: Data versioning â†’ Experiment tracking â†’ Model registry â†’ CI/CD pipelines â†’ Model monitoring â†’ Feedback loop. Azure ML supports all stages.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of splitting a dataset into training and test sets?

options.text: To make the dataset smaller and faster to process
To train the model on one portion and evaluate its performance on unseen data
To train two different models and compare them
To separate numeric features from categorical features

explanation.correct: The training set teaches the model. The test set evaluates how well the model performs on data it has never seen â€” simulating real-world performance and checking for overfitting.
explanation.incorrect: Splits don't reduce data size by default. Training two models is a different concept. Feature separation is preprocessing.
explanation.examTip: Typical splits: 80/20 or 70/30 (train/test). With validation: 60/20/20. Never use test data during training â€” it would give falsely optimistic results.

questions.questionText: What is a neural network in the context of deep learning?

options.text: A biological network of neurons in the human brain
A computational model inspired by the brain, consisting of interconnected layers of nodes that learn representations from data
A network of Azure AI services connected together
A decision tree with multiple branches

explanation.correct: An artificial neural network has an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each node applies a weighted function and activation. Deep learning = many hidden layers enabling automatic feature learning.
explanation.incorrect: This is artificial/computational, not biological. It's not an Azure architecture diagram or a decision tree.
explanation.examTip: Neural network layers: Input â†’ Hidden (1+ layers) â†’ Output. Deep = many hidden layers. Enables: image recognition, NLP, speech. Requires large data and compute.

questions.questionText: What is responsible AI impact assessment and why should it be done before deploying an AI system?

options.text: A financial cost analysis to determine if AI is cost-effective
A systematic evaluation of potential harms, biases, and ethical risks an AI system could cause to individuals and society
A technical performance benchmark comparing different models
A user satisfaction survey conducted after deployment

explanation.correct: A responsible AI impact assessment identifies potential harms (discrimination, privacy violations, safety risks, misuse) before deployment â€” enabling teams to mitigate risks proactively rather than reactively after harm has occurred.
explanation.incorrect: Not about costs, benchmarks, or post-deployment feedback. Impact assessment is pre-deployment risk analysis.
explanation.examTip: Microsoft responsible AI tooling: AI Fairness assessment (Fairlearn), model explainability (InterpretML), data profiling, impact assessment templates. All available in Azure ML.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes machine learning concepts.

statements.text: Unsupervised learning requires labelled training data.
A regression model predicts a continuous numeric value.
Feature engineering can significantly improve model performance.
A model with very high training accuracy always performs well in production.

explanation.correct: Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data. Regression predicts numbers (price, temperature). Feature engineering improves models significantly. High training accuracy can mean overfitting â€” poor production performance.
explanation.incorrect: Unsupervised = no labels needed. High training accuracy without good test accuracy = overfitting.
explanation.examTip: Never judge a model by training accuracy alone. Always check test/validation performance. Real-world performance depends on both.
